definition.text: A fishery is either the business of catching or raising fish and other aquatic life or, more often, the place where this happens, the fishing grounds.

facts.text: The FAO defines a fishery as an activity leading to harvesting fish, whether wild-caught or farmed.
A fishery is usually defined by its people, species, area, fishing method, class of boats and purpose.
In fisheries, 'fish' is a collective term that includes molluscs, crustaceans and any aquatic animal harvested for economic value.
About 500 million people worldwide depend economically on fisheries.
Close to 90% of catches come from oceans and seas; most marine fisheries lie near coasts where nutrients make fish abundant.
Fisheries were once 'first-come, first-served', but overfishing has forced more regulation.
Total fish production hit a record 171 million tonnes in 2016, 88% of it eaten directly by people.
A 2014 estimate put fisheries' contribution at US$270 billion a year to global GDP, with up to US$50 billion more possible from fully sustainable fishing.

definition.text: Fisheries are divided into commercial, recreational and subsistence sectors, and can be saltwater or freshwater, wild or farmed.

facts.text: Capture fisheries are broadly industrial, small-scale or artisanal, and recreational.
About 85% of marine fisheries production is finfish, mainly anchoveta, Alaska pollock and skipjack tuna.
Reduction fisheries, which process catch into products, are distinguished from others.

definition.text: Climate change affects fisheries through warming, acidifying and oxygen-poor oceans, and through altered temperatures, flows and habitats in fresh waters.

facts.text: It is shifting where fish live and how productive species are, changing the availability and trade of fish products.
The biggest falls in maximum catch potential are expected in the tropics, mostly in the South Pacific.
Global ocean catch is expected to fall 6 percent by 2100, and 11 percent in tropical zones.
Acidification makes it harder for shellfish, corals and zooplankton to build shells, putting 'cracks in the food chain'.
Overfished stocks, smaller and less genetically diverse, are more sensitive to climate stress.
Fish provides essential nutrition to 3 billion people, and poor, rural fishing communities are most exposed.
Fishing vessels caused about 0.5 percent of global CO2 emissions in 2012, 172.3 million tonnes.
Cutting fleet overcapacity and rebuilding stocks could raise resilience and returns by US$50 billion a year; removing fuel subsidies cuts both emissions and overfishing.

definition.text: Fisheries law is an emerging specialist field of law that studies fisheries management approaches such as catch shares and territorial use rights.

facts.text: It also covers international treaties, seafood safety, aquaculture and feed regulation, and access to justice for small-scale and aboriginal fishers.
The field is rarely taught at law schools, leaving a gap in advocacy and research.
The 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, in force from 1994, was one of the first such international laws.

title: Territorial use rights for fishing
article: Fisheries law#Territorial Use Rights for Fishing (TURF)

definition.text: Territorial use rights for fishing (TURFs) give communities or individuals exclusive fishing privileges over a defined area to prevent overexploitation.

facts.text: They usually go to communities with long traditions of sustainable fishing and are run by local fishers, with government-set conservation rules.
The most successful examples are in Chile and Japan; Chile has over 700 TURFs covering around 1100 square kilometres.
Because fishers depend on their own areas, they have an incentive to manage them sustainably.
Chile's TURFs for artisanal fisheries helped rebuild seabed fish stocks and raised fishers' compliance.
